The chunked shape: a parent RagDocuments table plus a child RagChunks table carrying the embeddings, because retrieval quality depends on chunking and chunks are the unit of both embedding and ranking
A separate database per document
Store embeddings in temp tables for speed

questions.explain: CAST is the honest path; TRY_CAST plus a quarantine table catches malformed rows in staging, and the chapter insists on parameterizing — never concatenating embedding JSON into dynamic SQL.
options: CAST the JSON string AS VECTOR(n) — strict, so wrong dimension counts fail loudly; in pipeline code use TRY_CAST and quarantine failures so one malformed vector never aborts a batch
Store the JSON as NVARCHAR(MAX) and compare strings
Convert with CONVERT(INT, ...) per element
Concatenate the JSON directly into dynamic SQL for speed

questions.explain: The right mental model: backfills of modest size and administrative re-embedding in the database; batched pipelines (Azure Functions, container jobs, ADF) for production ingestion at scale.
options: It builds DiskANN indexes automatically
It replaces the embedding model entirely
It is the fastest bulk-load path for millions of vectors

It lets T-SQL call an embedding API (e.g., Azure OpenAI) directly — genuinely useful for backfills, prototypes, and low-volume workloads — but it issues one HTTPS call per invocation, so production ingestion at scale belongs in a batched application pipeline

questions.explain: Stage-then-merge with batched commits bounds log growth and gives restartable checkpoints; index maintenance during bulk insert is pure overhead.
options: Row-by-row INSERTs in a single transaction
Keep the DiskANN index online during the load for validation

Stage raw JSON into an unindexed heap, quarantine malformed rows with TRY_CAST, then run batched typed INSERT...SELECT (commit every 5,000–10,000 rows) — dropping any DiskANN index before the load and rebuilding after
Load directly into the production table and fix errors later

Re-embed everything into a new column (or table) and cut over atomically — never mixing coordinate spaces in one column — since vectors from different models cannot be compared

Convert old vectors by multiplying by a constant
